title: Vintage Gibson Les Paul Junior Value Guide: Yearly Prices
description: Vintage Gibson Les Paul Junior values by year, with sunburst, cherry and TV Model references, original-part considerations and photos from my archive.
h1: Vintage Gibson Les Paul Junior Value Guide
alt: Sunburst body of a 1955 Gibson Les Paul Junior with one black pickup and a wraparound bridge

faqs.q: What Is A Vintage Gibson Les Paul Junior Worth?
faqs.a: The guide range for 1954 to 1958 sunburst single-cutaway Juniors is $6,000 to $13,000. The corresponding 1955 to 1958 single-cutaway TV Model range is $10,000 to $20,000. These assume all-original excellent condition with the original case; repairs and changed parts need a separate appraisal.

faqs.q: What Is A 1956 Gibson Les Paul Junior Worth?
faqs.a: A sunburst 1956 Junior falls within the shared 1954 to 1958 reference of $6,000 to $13,000. A single-cutaway TV Model uses the separate $10,000 to $20,000 reference. I need to confirm the finish, retained parts, condition and case before narrowing either range.

faqs.q: What Is A 1959 Cherry Les Paul Junior Worth?
faqs.a: An excellent, original rounded double-cutaway cherry Junior with its original case has a guide range of $10,500 to $13,500. I wouldn't apply that clean category automatically to a worn, repaired or incomplete guitar.

faqs.q: Is A TV Model The Same As A Les Paul Special?
faqs.a: No. The TV Model discussed here has one pickup and belongs with the Junior comparison. A Les Paul Special has two pickups and needs its own model comparison. TV Yellow alone doesn't establish which model you have.

faqs.q: Why Does This Table Stop Before 1979?
faqs.a: This table covers the earlier slab-body configuration. Later pointed SG-shaped Juniors belong in the SG Junior value guide, even if they retain Les Paul Junior lettering. I don't extend an earlier body's price range into years when a different configuration was the production model.

faqs.q: Does A Quality Refret Make A Junior Non-Original?
faqs.a: A quality refret is accepted maintenance and preserves the all-original classification of an otherwise all-original guitar. It takes the guitar out of the museum-quality category. Neck reshaping and a replaced fingerboard are separate alterations.

faqs.q: Does A Refinish Have A Fixed Percentage Deduction?
faqs.a: No. I assess the finish work together with the guitar's remaining original parts and any structural repairs. A single percentage can conceal the differences between an otherwise intact guitar and a heavily modified one.

faqs.q: Should I Replace Parts Before Asking For An Appraisal?
faqs.a: Document the guitar as it is and keep any removed original parts with it. I don't need you to reinstall hardware, disturb wiring or authorize cosmetic work before an initial appraisal. Clear photographs and the repair history you know are enough to start.
